# Audience map

Vantmoor writes for three audiences, and every public artifact should know which
one it is for before the first sentence is drafted.

**Operating practitioners** run analytics pipelines daily. They already know the
vocabulary, distrust vendor content by default, and reward specificity: an exact
failure mode, an exact measurement, an exact fix. Content for them can skip context
and must never explain basics they live with.

**Team leads** decide what their teams adopt. They know the problem space but not the
daily texture, so content for them opens with the operational consequence before the
mechanism. They forward content that makes them look well-informed; give them the
one-sentence version to forward.

**Evaluators** are actively comparing tools. They have read every vendor's claims and
are looking for disconfirming evidence; the fastest way to earn their trust is to
state plainly what the product does not do. Content for them names limitations
unprompted and links to checkable sources for every comparison.

When one artifact must serve several audiences, structure it so each can stop reading
at the depth they need: consequence first, mechanism second, operational detail last.
A piece that interleaves the three depths serves none of them.

## Anti-audiences

Two audiences are explicitly not written for: awards-and-buzz curators, whose
attention converts to nothing the company values, and hostile skim-readers hunting
for a quotable overreach. The first is ignored; the second is defended against by
the evidence standards themselves — a piece with no overreach offers nothing to
quote against us.
